study_description: Philip K. Dick's engagement with the Bible across the Exegesis, the letters, the interviews, the VALIS trilogy and the short fiction: the books he quoted, the translations and glosses he used, the readings he made of them, and the claim that developed across 1975–81 that the Bible is not a record of the past but a living text describing, and in some sense being, the present world.

featured_sections.title: What this study claims
body: Philip K. Dick read the Bible from his schooldays, by his own account in 1981. In the 1970s he began to read it as a text about his own time, and then, in the notebooks known as the Exegesis, as a text that was the world he was living in. This study follows that change through the sources the repository holds, and keeps each source in its own register.

The main evidence is the Exegesis: Dick's own words in 1,104 transcribed segments, of which 383 use Bible vocabulary at least once. The archive also holds the full text of his letters, of five interview transcripts, of the short stories, and of the VALIS chapters and other novels, so the same argument can be followed into correspondence, speech and fiction. Everything else is either editorial summary or secondary scholarship, and is labelled as such.

featured_sections.title: What the archive does not yet show
body: The 1974 Vertex interview is not held as text, so this study cannot say what Dick told that interviewer about scripture. The archive PDFs and the scholarship are searched as well, but only the letters, interviews, stories and novels have been read for cards.

A sweep matches words. It will miss an allusion to scripture that does not name the book, and it will find a word that does not mean the Bible. An absence of a card is therefore not a finding about Dick.

topic.canonical_name: The Bible in Philip K. Dick
topic.definition: Scripture as Dick read it: the books he quoted, the translations and glosses he used, and the readings he made. From 1975 he treated the Bible as a book of the future; by 1976 as code for the present; by 1981 as the world itself, and his own novels as a third testament.
topic.pkd_relevance: The Bible is the text Dick returned to for his whole life, and in the Exegesis it becomes the frame for his theory of reality. The shift from text to world is the main movement in his late thought, and the trilogy shows it as a scene.
topic.in_the_fiction: VALIS and The Divine Invasion hold the Bible as characters’ argument and as a hologram. The Divine Invasion gives the Torah a speaker, Zina Pallas. The short stories hold it in passing: as a question a character asks, as a dream image, and as a phrase a man reaches for when he has been where others have not come back.
topic.in_the_exegesis: The sweep finds Bible vocabulary in 383 of the 1,104 transcribed segments. The argument runs through the 1975 batch, the 15 September 1976 sitting on Acts in Tears, the 1978 folder on the living Torah and the Bible in three dimensions, and the April 1981 transcriptions on recombinant scripture and the third testament.
topic.intellectual_background: Dick’s reference works are named in the transcriptions: the Jerusalem Bible and its notes, a “Decoded New Testament”, and Augustine’s image of the Bible as letters from home. In the letters he reads the Torah with the notes of J. H. Hertz. The Hymn of the Pearl, in the apocryphal Acts of Thomas, is the one Gnostic text the scholarship traces through him.
topic.scholarly_debate: Scholars reach the Bible in Dick through its Gnostic and Pauline edges. The debate is whether his use of scripture is theology or a literary device; the Exegesis argues the first, and the trilogy often stages the second.
topic.chronology_summary: 1964: a priest’s reading in a letter. 1972: the Bible in rhymed couplets, begun as a joke. 1975: the Bible as a book of the future, and as cypher. September 1976: Acts in Tears, and the Bible as code for the present. 1978: the living Torah and the Bible in three dimensions. 1980–81: the Torah as Holy Wisdom, recombinant scripture, and the Bible as information. April 1981: the Bible as the real world, and a third testament.
topic.contradictions_summary: Dick never settles whether the Bible is a record of the past or a description of the present. In 1976 it is “not about the past”; in 1978 the Torah is timeless; in 1981 the Bible is “the real world”.
topic.editorial_notes: Hand-authored editorial prose. The sweep is the corpus; the cards are the passages chosen from it; the prose cites cards and quotes only what the corpus contains. The letters are the full text of the Selected Letters volumes, except the 1972 letter, which is quoted from the excerpt file. The interviews are transcripts, and their cards quote Dick’s own speech. The stories are full text, and their cards quote characters, which is lane A as fiction. The scholarship and the archive PDFs are searched but not yet carded. Folder dates are batch dates.
open_questions: What did Dick say about the Bible at the 1974 Vertex interview? Resolvable by: a transcript. None is held as text.

Which Bible did he use? The transcriptions name the Jerusalem Bible and a “Decoded New Testament”, but not an edition of the first or the source of the second. Resolvable by: an inventory of his library, if one survives.
Did Dick know the Acts material in Tears before 1974? He says he recognised it only after the novel appeared. Resolvable by: the manuscript or typescript of Flow My Tears, the Policeman Said.
What do the letters of 1982 say about scripture? They are held in full, and no card from that year has been chosen yet.
What do the scholarship and the archive PDFs add? Resolvable by: reading the lane C hits in the sweep, and deciding the lane of the published Exegesis, which the database records as B.

dossier_sections.heading: The Bible in Philip K. Dick
body: For the last years of his life Philip K. Dick argued that the Bible is not a record of the past but a text about the present, and that he was living inside it. This study follows that argument through the sources the repository holds, and keeps each source in its own register.

The strongest evidence is still the Exegesis, Dick’s own notebooks, transcribed here as 1,104 segments. A sweep of their raw text finds Bible vocabulary in 383 of them: the Bible, Scripture, the Testaments, the Gospels, the Torah, and named books and verses. The archive also holds the full text of 1,175 letters from the Selected Letters volumes, of the short stories, of the VALIS chapters and other novels, and of five interview transcripts. Dick’s letters, speech and fiction are cited in lane A, and fiction is marked as fiction. The novel and story summaries, the Exegesis analysis and the scholarship are editorial or secondary, and are labelled where they are used.

Two limits remain. The 1974 Vertex interview is not held as text. And the sweep matches words: a passage that alludes to scripture without naming it will not be found, so an absence here is an absence of the word.

dossier_sections.heading: 1964: a priest’s reading
body: The earliest Bible passage in the letters is from May 1964, when Dick wrote to James Blish about his priest and about God’s absence. “My priest says the Bible is not the story of man's search for God but of God's search for man.” {{BIB-LET-64-01}} Dick sets the line against his own inability to see the Redeemer, and asks where He has gone. It reads the Bible from God’s side.

dossier_sections.heading: 1972: the Bible in rhymed couplets
body: In 1972 the Bible first becomes a project, and it begins as a joke. On 1 December Dick wrote to Roger Zelazny about a dream in which he was given an award, and learned that the award was for this: “I had set the Bible into rhymed couplets.” {{BIB-LET-72-01}}

He gave a sample: “In the beginning God separated the water from the land, And exclaimed, ‘My, isn’t that grand.’” He preferred Luther’s rendering of the line “And God saw that it good was.” The letter treats the Bible first as language, something to be translated, parodied and preferred.

dossier_sections.heading: 1973: the project under way
body: By January 1973 the joke has become a method. Dick calls the work the project “nearest and dearest to my heart”, and reports that it is “coming along fine, with the first one already firmly jelled and on paper.” {{BIB-LET-73-01}}

dossier_sections.heading: 1975: the Bible as a book of the future
body: In the February 1975 transcriptions the Bible is a prophetic text, and Dick states its time plainly: “The Bible is a book of the future.” {{BIB-EX-75-01}} The Old Testament gets less from him. “All the O.T. has in it is monotheism, which they got from Iknaton.” {{BIB-EX-75-02}}

By November the Bible has stopped being a source and become a condition of perception. “The world of the Bible was suddenly around me, and real, replacing our world.” {{BIB-EX-75-03}} The sentence that follows it gives the principle: “The book the Bible is an analog of reality.” {{BIB-EX-75-04}}
His working reference is the Jerusalem Bible, which he calls the “J. Bible”, and whose notes give him Rome as “the great and only real enemy of the new chosen people, the Church.” {{BIB-EX-75-05}}

The letters of the same year make the cypher claim in plain terms. To Robert Ornstein, in March, Dick writes that a character who studies the Bible with a Qumran figure “finds that the New Testament is in cypher.” {{BIB-LET-75-01}} In July, to Göran Bengtson, he describes the moment at which, in his account, “this is indeed the moment foretold in the Bible”, and the Parousia has arrived, though not in the form anyone had expected. {{BIB-LET-75-02}}

dossier_sections.heading: September 1976: the letters on the same ground
body: Nine days before the sitting on Acts in Tears, Dick tells Dorothy Hudner that “the prophecies of the Bible are all true and are systematically being fulfilled.” {{BIB-LET-76-01}} The evil spirit is in Rome, which is “the Prince of This World”, and the Parousia is not far off.

dossier_sections.heading: September 1976: Acts in Tears
body: The sitting of 15 September 1976 is the longest Bible argument in the Exegesis, and its first claim is that Flow My Tears, the Policeman Said, which the notebooks call “Tears”, contains “unmistakable material from Acts.” {{BIB-EX-76-01}} Acts, in his account, is the book of the early church, and it describes the period just after Christ leaves.

The claim comes with a difficulty that Dick records himself. Father Rasch pointed out the scene of Philip and the black man to him, “my first clue to biblical material in the book”, and Dick says he “had never read Acts”. {{BIB-EX-76-02}} He then asks how he could have identified the Acts elements the month the novel came out, if he had not recognised them when he wrote it. {{BIB-EX-76-03}}

The answer he reaches is that the world the novel describes is the world of Acts. “The true world is that of Acts. Why Acts? The last period of the scriptures, the time of the paraclete.” {{BIB-EX-76-04}} The same sitting calls Ubik a form of scripture, because the novel was, in his account, written by its own title. {{BIB-EX-76-05}}

dossier_sections.heading: 15 September 1976: the Bible as code
body: The sitting also makes the claim that organises the rest of his Bible writing. “In the Bible isn’t about the past; it’s code to describe our world (as is ‘Tears’).” {{BIB-EX-76-06}} The prophecy of Malachi gives him the timetable. “The ending of Malachi makes it absolutely clear that God (1) foresaw the ABSENCE of Elijah from the world”, and the return of Elijah is therefore part of a plan. {{BIB-EX-76-07}}

dossier_sections.heading: 1977: a conversion, and its reading
body: Dick dates his conversion experience to March 1974. Writing to Eugene Warren in August 1977, he says that since then he has read the Bible, the New Testament particularly, “again and again.” {{BIB-LET-77-01}} The letter says that two parts of what was revealed to him seemed the most striking, and one of them is the Jerusalem Bible’s note on Ephesians 1:10.

dossier_sections.heading: 1978: the living Torah
body: The folder dated 10 October 1978 is a batch date. Its entries refer to late 1980, so the folder is a sitting, not a day, and the argument in it develops across the years that follow. The Torah takes the place Acts held in 1976. “I am sure that the plasmate – & hence the cypher in ‘Tears’ – is the Living Torah, the informational basis of reality.” {{BIB-EX-78-01}}

The Torah is not, in this account, simply the Jewish law. It is the source that Christ corrects. “Jesus was the greatest of the Hebrew prophets, yet he was rejected by Israel. Why? Because he depreciated the Torah.” {{BIB-EX-78-02}} The cost to Dick’s own faith is stated in the same folder: “herewith I just lost my Trinitarianism!” {{BIB-EX-78-03}}
The programme is also stated. The third age has its own Torah, and “New Scriptures are needed, new prophets and perhaps a new savior.” {{BIB-EX-78-04}}

dossier_sections.heading: 1978: the Bible as code, and in three dimensions
body: What the Torah does for the cypher, VALIS does for the book. Dick proposes that the world of 1970–74 was built on information contained in the Bible, and “that Valis turned that info into our world.” {{BIB-EX-78-05}} The Bible then becomes an instrument as well as a source: “using the Bible as a encoding-decoding grid.” {{BIB-EX-78-06}}

The image he uses for it is spatial. “My visualizing the Bible in 3-D: layers according to age (time as spacial axis)” {{BIB-EX-78-07}} is the picture the trilogy later puts on the screen of Elias’s holoscope. See the Divine Invasion section below.

dossier_sections.heading: 1980–1981: the Torah as Wisdom, and the Bible as information
body: In February 1980 Dick tells Jonathan Silverman that he has discovered “that the Torah can be equated with Holy Wisdom (Hagia Sophia) of Proverbs 8.” {{BIB-LET-80-01}} The Torah he read with the notes of Hertz has become the Wisdom that existed before creation.

The 1981 letters give the Exegesis’s terms to correspondents. In July, to Patricia Warrick: “We have what I call recombinant information/scripture.” {{BIB-LET-81-01}} In August he sends her the fullest account: “The Bible is the information that is fed into the space-time universe, as if transduced into substantial reality.” {{BIB-LET-81-02}} A single coherent life form, he says, underlies the written Bible, and is “not fixed into a canon.” {{BIB-LET-81-03}}

Two letters of 1981 turn the same material on fiction and on ethics. To Russell Galen, in June, Dick says that Tim Archer “completely misuses the Bible”, and uses it “not as a man of God but as a lawyer.” {{BIB-LET-81-04}} To Ursula Le Guin, in August, he writes that the Torah “has enchanted me with its haunting concern for all creatures, especially the weak, the harmless and the disadvantaged.” {{BIB-LET-81-05}}

dossier_sections.heading: April 1981: the Bible is the real world
body: By April 1981 the claim has reversed. The Bible is no longer a description of the world, but the world: “the Bible is not a verbal description of a world; it is a world.” {{BIB-EX-81-01}}

The boy who read it is part of the argument. Dick says that when he was in junior high school and first read the Bible, “it was the O.T. that I read, not the N.T., esp. the part about Elijah.” {{BIB-EX-81-02}} The test he sets for any account of reality is a Bible test: “the touchstone (oh please do not forget this!) is the Bible.” {{BIB-EX-81-03}}

The working example is Acts again, now read against Luke. The “infinity” mode of 1974 was “the world of the Bible, specifically Acts – the 2nd half of Luke.” {{BIB-EX-81-04}} The image that carries the claim is Augustine’s. “Augustine called the Bible ‘Letters from home’.” {{BIB-EX-81-05}}

dossier_sections.heading: April 1981: recombinant scripture and a third testament
body: A closed canon is no longer possible on this account. Dick’s term for its replacement is “recombinant scripture”, which has “no canon, no precedent; each person + situation unique.” {{BIB-EX-81-06}}

He calls the revelation he is living a third testament: an “unprecedented third testament emanating out of the O.T. + N.T.” {{BIB-EX-81-07}} The hierarchy is stated in the same transcription: “Torah does not know everything. Christ does.” {{BIB-EX-81-08}} The law is the frame of the world, and Christ is the one who acts within it. That is the argument of the 1978 passages, put in its final form.

dossier_sections.heading: The interviews: what Dick said about scripture
body: Five interview transcripts are now held as text, and they change the record of what Dick said in public. In one conversation, printed in The Last Interview, he recalls his boyhood: “I started reading the Bible and I read that part about Elijah.” {{BIB-INT-06}} The same reading is in the Exegesis of April 1981, which records that it was “the O.T. that I read, not the N.T., esp. the part about Elijah.” {{BIB-EX-81-02}} In the same conversation the interviewer asks who John the Baptist was, and Dick answers from Malachi: “John the Baptist was Elijah.” {{BIB-INT-05}}

In His Own Words, Gregg Rickman’s book of 1984, has the most developed account. Dick says he studied the Torah until he understood its underlying themes, and that he has “switched from Christianity to Judaism.” {{BIB-INT-04}} {{BIB-INT-07}} In the compiled magazine interviews the same study is given to a novel: the resolution, he says, is “in terms of Judaism”, and he made “a very detailed study of the Torah and the basic tenets of Judaism for it.” {{BIB-INT-01}}

The compiled magazine interviews also have Dick reading Deuteronomy with the notes of Rabbi Hertz: “I was reading Deuteronomy last night.” {{BIB-INT-02}} The voice that guided him he names as Ruah, “the Old Testament word for the Spirit of God.” {{BIB-INT-03}}

The Missouri Review interview of 1984 is held in full. Its few Bible hits are mostly names, but Dick says the title A Scanner Darkly comes from Paul’s “through a glass, darkly.” {{BIB-INT-08}} The 1974 Vertex interview is not held at all, so what Dick said there about scripture cannot be checked.

dossier_sections.heading: What the trilogy does with the Bible
body: In VALIS the Bible is a problem that characters argue over. Sherri, the sceptic, asks whether a passage Fat has quoted is “one of the corrupt parts of the Bible”. {{BIB-TR-VAL-01}} Kevin, who becomes a convert, reads Daniel for Nixon: “Now Kevin had become a Bible scholar, to Fat’s amusement.” {{BIB-TR-VAL-02}} Fat traces Psalm 104 to Akhenaten’s hymn, and says the hymn “entered our Bible—it’s older than our Bible.” {{BIB-TR-VAL-03}}

The Divine Invasion takes the Exegesis’s three-dimensional Bible and gives it a scene. Elias’s holoscope lays out “the Bible expressed as layers at different depths within the hologram, each layer according to age.” {{BIB-TR-DI-01}} Scripture in the hologram “became a sentient organism that was never twice the same.” {{BIB-TR-DI-02}} The Torah is the same living thing the notebooks describe: “Torah is the totality of divine disclosure by God; it is alive; it existed before creation.” {{BIB-TR-DI-03}}

The novel gives the Torah a body. Zina Pallas says: “I am the Torah.” {{BIB-TR-DI-04}} Emmanuel, the boy at the centre of the novel, wants to add a line of his own to the Bible’s hologram, and does not: “He wanted to feed that into the hologram of the Bible, as an addendum, but he knew that he should not.” {{BIB-TR-DI-05}} In the notebooks Dick is sure of his right to add to scripture. In the novel the right is withheld.

dossier_sections.heading: The stories, as full text
body: The short stories are now held as full text, and the Bible is in them, mostly in passing. The stories give scripture to characters, as a phrase they reach for. In “A Terran Odyssey” a character asks of a strange light, “Is it God? You know, like in the Bible.” {{BIB-STO-01}} In “The Eye of the Sibyl” a dream of open books is “even holy, like the Bible.” {{BIB-STO-03}} In “A Little Something for Us Tempunauts” a character who has already been where the others are going thinks: “We all go to one place, he thought, as the Bible says.” {{BIB-STO-05}}

In “Not by Its Cover” a character suggests binding a copy of the Bible in wub-fur, and another says he had it done and read Paul’s letters to the Corinthians in it. {{BIB-STO-02}} In “Retreat Syndrome” one man tells another to leave Carol alone: “Look it up in the Bible if you don't believe me.” {{BIB-STO-04}} These are the characters’ words, read in lane A as fiction. None of them is Dick’s own argument.

dossier_sections.heading: The other novels, as summarised
body: The novel summaries follow the same pattern. The Bible appears in the summaries of The Divine Invasion and VALIS, and in The Transmigration of Timothy Archer, where a character quotes scripture. The summary of Ubik records a biblical tradition of dreams. The summaries of Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, The Man in the High Castle and A Maze of Death record no biblical reference. These are summaries of summaries, useful for orientation and not evidence in their own right.
Some novels are also held as full text, and the sweep finds Bible references in that text. This study has not yet carded them.

dossier_sections.heading: What the scholarship says
body: Scholars have reached the Bible in Dick’s work mainly through its Gnostic and Pauline edges. Davis follows the Hymn of the Pearl, which is “embedded in the third-century Acts of Thomas”, through Dick’s engagement with it from 1975. {{BIB-SCH-01}} The Acts there are apocryphal, and the canonical Acts of the 1976 sitting are a different book.

Burton reads Dick’s fiction against Bergson and against “the theology of Saint Paul”. {{BIB-SCH-02}} The archive’s record of the VALIS appendix names “Paul of Tarsus, Simon Magus” among those said to have known a great secret. {{BIB-SCH-03}} The scholarship is also held as full text, and the sweep finds biblical references in it. This study has carded only the records that bear on Dick’s own words, so the scholarship is thin here, and a full reading of it is still to do.

dossier_sections.heading: What the Bible meant to Dick
body: Three things were true of the Bible for Dick, and the archive supports each of them. It was a text he read closely, in translation and with commentary, from the Jerusalem Bible notes to the “Decoded New Testament” he was rereading in 1975. It was a rival authority: Acts is the true world, Christ corrects the Torah, and in 1981 the Torah “does not know everything”. And it was a model for his own writing: Tears is read as Acts, Ubik as scripture, and the trilogy as a third testament.

What did not settle is whether the Bible describes the past or the present. In 1976 it is “not about the past”. In 1978 the Torah is the timeless source of the informational world. In 1981 the Bible is “the real world”, and Dick’s own novels belong to a new testament. The contradictions run through the whole sequence, and this essay does not resolve them.

The lanes differ in voice. The trilogy and the stories give the Bible to characters who argue about it: Sherri, Kevin, Emmanuel, who holds back, and the men in the stories who reach for a line. The Exegesis gives it to one reader who is sure of his reading. The letters give it to correspondents, in the voice of a friend: in 1981 Dick explains the Bible to Patricia Warrick as information, a life form and a canon that has gone. That difference of voice is the clearest thing the lanes show side by side.
